- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., >0.7) and forecast is rising, reduce overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to short-term momentum.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.3) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — add 3–5% to prevent premature bottoming.  
- If recent price action shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of price decline after a spike), model should adjust forecast downward with a lag of 1–2 days.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), forecast should not immediately revert — allow 2–3 days of “cooling” before adjusting downward.  
- If sentiment is volatile (e.g., alternating +/–0.3 or more), reduce forecast confidence — use a smoother moving average or dampen volatility in forecast curve.  
- For long-term (30-day) forecasts, if true outcome deviates >3% from 14-day moving average, adjust forecast to align with recent trend, not just last 18 days.  
- When sentiment is neutral or weak (e.g., 0.0–0.3), forecast should not be overly sensitive to short-term noise — use 30-day average as baseline.  
- If true outcome consistently under/over-predicts by >2% over 3–5 consecutive days, adjust forecast horizon to 28-day or 35-day window to reduce lag.
